citation.authors: Linux man-pages project; systemd project; UAPI Group
citation.title: hier(7) (Linux man-pages 6.19); file-hierarchy(7) (systemd); UAPI.9 Linux File System Hierarchy

claims.planned: Linux-specific descriptions of the tree incl. /run, /proc, /sys; /usr merge (bin -> usr/bin symlinks) on modern distros
claims.finding: Two corrections. (1) hier(7) (man-pages 6.19) describes /run, /proc and /sys but says NOTHING about the /usr merge; it still describes /bin and /sbin as separate directories, following FHS 3.0. (2) file-hierarchy(7) on man7.org is now a three-sentence stub (systemd 262~devel): the content moved to the UAPI Group spec 'UAPI.9 Linux File System Hierarchy', which is where the merge is documented as 'Compatibility Symlinks'. Debian's bookworm release notes state merged-/usr is now required. Verified by running: on ubuntu:24.04 and debian:bookworm-slim /bin -> usr/bin, /sbin -> usr/sbin, /lib -> usr/lib; alpine:3.20 is NOT merged (/bin, /sbin, /lib are real directories). Note UAPI.9 goes further than Ubuntu/Debian: it also lists /usr/sbin as a symlink to /usr/bin, which Ubuntu 24.04 does not do (/sbin -> usr/sbin).
claims.quote: These compatibility symlinks point to /usr/bin/, ensuring that scripts and binaries referencing these legacy paths correctly find their binaries.
claims.location: UAPI.9 Linux File System Hierarchy, 'Compatibility Symlinks: /bin/; /sbin/; /usr/sbin/'

extra_findings.fact: file-hierarchy(7) is now a pointer page.
extra_findings.quote: Operating systems using the systemd(1) system and service manager are organized based on a file system hierarchy inspired by UNIX, as described in UAPI.9 Linux File System Hierarchy[1].

Debian has adopted a filesystem layout, referred to as "merged-/usr", which no longer includes the legacy directories /bin, /sbin, /lib, or optional variants such as /lib64. In the new layout, the legacy directories are replaced with symlinks to the corresponding locations /usr/bin, /usr/sbin, /usr/lib, and /usr/lib64.
extra_findings.location: Debian 12 release notes 5.1.14 'A "merged-/usr" is now required'

extra_findings.quote:
ubuntu:24.04 $ ls -ld /bin /sbin /lib -> lrwxrwxrwx ... /bin -> usr/bin ; /lib -> usr/lib ; /sbin -> usr/sbin
debian:bookworm-slim: identical symlinks
alpine:3.20: drwxr-xr-x /bin, /lib, /sbin (real directories; /bin/sh, /bin/ls, /usr/bin/timeout -> /bin/busybox)
This directory contains information which describes the system since it was booted. Once this purpose was served by /var/run and programs may continue to use it.
This is a mount point for the proc filesystem, which provides information about running processes and the kernel. This pseudo-filesystem is described in more detail in proc(5).
This is a mount point for the sysfs filesystem, which provides information about the kernel like /proc, but better structured, following the formalism of kobject infrastructure.
This directory contains temporary files which may be deleted with no notice, such as by a regular job or at system boot up.
Like /tmp, this directory holds temporary files stored for an unspecified duration.
This directory is usually mounted from a separate partition. It should hold only shareable, read-only data, so that it can be mounted by various machines running Linux.

/usr/bin This is the primary directory for executable programs. ... /usr/local This is where programs which are local to the site typically go. ... /var/log Miscellaneous log files. ... /opt This directory should contain add-on packages that contain static files.

extra_findings.fact: hier(7) /etc/skel — where a new user's dotfiles come from.
extra_findings.quote: When a new user account is created, files from this directory are usually copied into the user's home directory.

extra_findings.fact: hier(7) admits it is not authoritative for any given box, and cites FHS 3.0 as its standard.
extra_findings.quote: This list is not exhaustive; different distributions and systems may be configured differently.

extra_findings.fact: UAPI.9 /tmp: usually a tmpfs, small files only, flushed at boot, may be aged out; honour $TMPDIR.
extra_findings.quote: The place for small temporary files. This directory is usually mounted as a tmpfs instance, and should hence not be used for larger files. (Use /var/tmp/ for larger files.) This directory is usually flushed at boot-up. Also, files that are not accessed within a certain time may be automatically deleted.

The place for larger and persistent temporary files. In contrast to /tmp/, this directory is usually mounted from a persistent physical file system and can thus accept larger files. ... This directory is generally not flushed at boot-up, but time-based cleanup of files that have not been accessed for a certain time is applied.
A tmpfs file system for system packages to place runtime data, socket files, and similar. This directory is flushed on boot, and generally writable for privileged programs only. Always writable.

Vendor-supplied operating system resources. Usually read-only, but this is not required. Possibly shared between multiple hosts. This directory should not be modified by the administrator, except when installing or removing vendor-supplied packages.
extra_findings.location: UAPI.9, /usr/ (and /etc/: 'System-specific configuration. This directory may be read-only.')

extra_findings.fact: UAPI.9 /proc and /sys are kernel APIs, and /sys is normally read-only in containers — directly relevant to sandbox audits.
extra_findings.quote: A virtual kernel file system exposing discovered devices and other functionality. This file system is mostly an API to interface with the kernel and not a place where normal files may be stored. In sandboxed/containerized setups, this directory is generally mounted read-only.

Place for POSIX shared memory segments, as created via shm_open(3). This directory is flushed on boot, and is a tmpfs file system. Since all users have write access to this directory, special care should be taken to avoid name clashes and vulnerabilities.

extra_findings.fact: UAPI.9 /var/run is a compatibility symlink to /run.
extra_findings.quote: This compatibility symlink points to /run/, ensuring that programs referencing this legacy path correctly find their runtime data.

teaching_notes: The planned claim needs re-sourcing: hier(7) does not mention the /usr merge at all, and file-hierarchy(7) has been hollowed out into a pointer to the UAPI Group's UAPI.9 spec (cite it as https://uapi-group.org/specifications/specs/linux_file_system_hierarchy/ with a tag such as [UAPI.9] if quoting it). For 'modern distros are usr-merged' cite the Debian 12 release notes plus the executed ls -ld output; and teach that Alpine is the counter-example (unmerged, BusyBox symlinks). UAPI.9 is more useful than hier(7) for container work because it states operational properties (tmpfs /tmp and /run, read-only /usr and /sys in containers). Added sources beyond the planned URLs: UAPI.9 and the Debian bookworm release notes (both primary).
